extracted.intended_audience: federal judges and litigating lawyers handling unfair-competition/news-misappropriation cases (Associated Press v. International News Service style disputes)
extracted.subtask_description: Defendant's appellate/trial brief arguing why complainant's proofs fail to establish unlawful use of Associated Press materials and why equitable relief (injunction) should be denied. Focuses on evidentiary sufficiency, industry practices, and equitable doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific-evidence requirement for accusations of improper use of membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant's proofs totally fail to establish the accusation that defendant 'has made improper and unconscionable use of the memberships held in the complainant' — scarcely one word of evidence shown; general 'informed and believes' statements without sources are inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits must present concrete, particularized instances showing improper use; bald assertions or hearsay phrased as 'informed and believes' are insufficient to support the claim or equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits must show actual use, not mere observation or assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing an editor 'read over sheets' or make notes, or an employe 'examining Associated Press copy', does not by itself establish that defendant used complainant's news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence should link observed copying/reading/notes to actual use in defendant's output. Anti-pattern: assuming reading = unlawful use. Courts require proof that notes/extracts were employed by defendant, not merely taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and distinction of 'tips' versus 'dispatches'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'tip' in news-service parlance means a dispatch containing, in a brief manner, the substance of the nature and character of a story and frequently indicates its point or origin. Witnesses distinguish 'tips' from full 'dispatches.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating charges about 'tips', clarify whether the allegation concerns brief tips (industry-norm) or transmittal of full dispatches. Evidence and remedies differ depending on which was transmitted and how it was obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility of 'independent investigation' given timing of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant claims independent investigation after receiving tips; defendant argues that stories appearing over complainant's wires within minutes of a tip make such independent investigation implausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess timing between receipt of tip and publication; near-immediate publication undermines claims that independent verification occurred before use. Use chronology to test credibility of 'independent investigation' defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable doctrine: clean hands (requiring plaintiff's good conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: He who comes into equity must come with clean hands — if complainant itself engages in the same practices it objects to, equity may deny relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate complainant's conduct; if it has practiced obtaining or using 'tips' similarly, the court may refuse equitable remedies. Cite controlling equitable precedents where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction limited to tips obtained through breach of trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant expresses willingness to refrain from obtaining tips only insofar as such tips are 'obtained through the breach of some trust relation', which it admits would be improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relief should target only tips procured by a breach of duty/trust (e.g., bribery, corruption), not the general, non-fraudulent exchange/use of tips. Draft injunctions narrowly to that scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality constraint: injunctions would be operationally intolerable
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction requiring an investigation into the origin and source of every news tip would impose intolerable hardship and could make news businesses impossible, since by the time investigation concludes the information may no longer be news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should weigh operational impracticability and the perishable nature of news when considering broad prophylactic injunctive relief; narrower remedies are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published bulletins and early editions become public property
rubrics_metrics.description: When bulletins and early editions are published the news therein becomes public property and available to the world at large for all purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material that has been publicly published (bulletins/early editions) cannot be restrained as confidential proprietary matter; defendant may lawfully rewrite and distribute such publicly available news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's equitable standing undermined if it engages in same practices
rubrics_metrics.description: If complainant is engaged in doing the same thing it seeks to prevent, it may lack standing in a court of equity to enjoin defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether complainant's own policies/practices mirror the complained-of conduct; use that to argue lack of equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-zealous employee doctrine — absence of corporate knowledge/consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrongdoing of an over-zealous employee in excess of his authority should not automatically be imputed to the defendant corporation if there was no knowledge or consent by the employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To hold the employer liable, show that corporate officers knew of, approved, or authorized the wrongful conduct; otherwise treat as unauthorized individual misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity requirement for affidavits (dates, names, specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits that use vague language ('repeatedly', unnamed 'one of the editors') or fail to state whether sheets contained fresh news are weak and non-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiants should provide explicit particulars: who, when, exactly what was read/copied, whether it was unpublished, and how it was used. Lack of particulars reduces evidentiary weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay/failure to notify affected members weakens claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses observed alleged acts long before the suit and complainant did not make prior complaint to the member (e.g., New York American); first knowledge only upon moving papers undermines allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely notice to affected members and prompt complaints bolster credibility; prolonged silence or delay supports defense arguments of laches or lack of material harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to show that copying led to subsequent use by defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony that a defendant's employe made copies/extracts is not enough; plaintiff must show that those copies or notes were used by defendant in its publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link copying events to specific uses (published stories, reproductions) to prove actionable misappropriation rather than mere access or curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity to trace origin/source of tips when alleging improper obtaining
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove improper obtaining, the plaintiff must show where tips originated and that they were procured through improper means (e.g., from complainant's dispatches or by breach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should attempt to trace the flow of information (who sent tips, through what channel, and whether a trust was breached) rather than relying on inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry practice and internal policies temper claims of impropriety
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence shows Associated Press itself used and encouraged 'tips' (operators authorized and credited for sending tips); this practice is nationwide and longstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand prevailing industry norms and internal directives (e.g., manager memos crediting tips) when assessing whether particular conduct is improper; widespread accepted practice weakens claims of unconscionability.
